transmission rates. Such retail financial commitments alone fail to protect other wholesale 
transmission customers from the risk of unreasonably bearing substantial stranded transmission 
costs caused if those large loads fail to show up as expected, whether initially or after the load goes 
into service.
I.
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO RESPOND
The Commission’s Rules prohibit answers to answers unless otherwise authorized,4 but the 
Commission has the authority to waive this prohibition for good cause.5 It routinely grants motions 
for leave to answer when doing so will assist the Commission’s decision-making process.6 The 
following Response will aid the Commission’s understanding of the range of risks and concerns 
regarding new, large load interconnections, such as large data center loads. 
II.
LIMITED RESPONSE
For the reasons described in our earlier comments in the now-consolidated proceedings, 
Buckeye disagrees with many of Vistra’s arguments on the treatment of co-location arrangements7 
but responds only to Vistra’s discussion of potential requirements for “financial commitments” by 
new large loads.8 Vistra’s Answer regarding this issue addresses earlier comments by Americans 
for a Clean Energy Grid (“ACEG”),9 which “proposed to require load-serving entities and electric 
4 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2).
5 Id. § 385.101(e).
6 See, e.g., Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 178 FERC ¶ 61,249, P 16 (2022) (accepting answers to answers 
“because they have provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process”).
7 See Comments of Buckeye Power, Inc. (Apr. 23, 2025), eLibrary 20250423-5154 (“Buckeye April 2025 
Comments”); Comments of Buckeye Power, Inc. (Dec. 9, 2024), eLibrary No. 20241209-5210 (“Buckeye December 
2024 Comments”). Not addressing these other issues does not imply agreement or waiver of any argument.  
8 Vistra Answer at 12-13. 
9 Comments of Americans for a Clean Energy Grid (Apr. 23, 2025), eLibrary No. 20250423-5217 (“ACEG 
Comments”).

- 4 -
distribution companies that request load adjustments demonstrate that any new large loads 
interconnections are backed by stringent financial commitments.”10 The idea behind such financial 
commitments is to “place the risk of customer-specific forecasting inaccuracy on the individual 
customer,”11 rather than the load-serving entity (“LSE”). Although “Vistra agrees that requiring 
such financial commitments would help improve the accuracy of PJM’s load forecasting by 
disincentivizing load customers from submitting multiple duplicative interconnection requests,” it 
argues that such reforms would need to be included in PJM’s Tariff and should be explored by the 
Commission in a separate proceeding.12
Buckeye agrees that retail financial commitments can play a useful role in improving 
forecast accuracy and protecting the host LSE and its own retail customers from the excessive 
transmission costs associated with overestimating new large loads.13 However, Vistra’s Answer 
(like ACEG’s Comments to which Vistra responds) fails to recognize that the risks of inaccurate 
forecasting go beyond just the allocation of risk between the host LSE and large end-use customer. 
As presented, the financial commitments concept omits one critically important element needed to 
protect other transmission customers from bearing stranded transmission costs when large loads 
fail to materialize as forecasted. To meet its Federal Power Act obligations, the Commission 
should take additional actions to fill this problematic void. 
10 Vistra Answer at 12. See also ACEG Comments at 3-4 and Attachment. 
11 ACEG Comments, Attach. at 2. 
12 Vistra Answer at 12-13. 
13 See Buckeye April 2025 Comments at 12 (explaining that LSEs can enter into arrangements with large end-use 
customers “e.g., through a minimum demand charge, and minimum contract term, backed by appropriate credit 
support requirement” to encourage end-use customer loads to show up as expected).  Buckeye takes no position on 
whether the requirement for forecasted load to be backed by “financial commitments” needs to be approved through 
a separate Commission proceeding or can be addressed through revisions to PJM’s manuals without FERC approval.

- 5 -
Specifically, as explained in Buckeye’s earlier comments in greater detail, wholesale 
transmission customers other than the host LSE face significant risks of stranded costs if large 
loads do not materialize as forecast.14 The costs of the significant transmission investments needed 
to serve new, large loads are shared among LSEs in the relevant PJM zone on a load-ratio share 
basis pursuant to transmission owner (“TO”) formula rates filed as Attachment H to the PJM 
OATT. If the large loads do not materialize, the host LSE’s load does not increase (or may 
subsequently decrease before the cost of transmission facilities built to serve the customer are fully 
recovered through rates, even if the large load initially went into service at planned-for levels), and 
a portion of the costs of transmission facilities built by the applicable transmission owner to serve 
the large load would thus be shifted to other LSEs in the TO Zone. Although retail “financial 
commitments” described by Vistra and ACEG may allow the host LSE to recover costs from the 
large load that failed to materialize (and potentially protect its retail customers), in the absence of 
further Commission action resulting in the crediting of the benefits of these financial commitments 
against the FERC jurisdictional wholesale transmission revenue requirement, the benefits of these 
“financial commitments” would be trapped at the host LSE’s retail level alone and would do 
nothing to protect other wholesale LSEs in the applicable TO Zone or their retail customers from 
these stranded transmission costs. 
To ensure just and reasonable wholesale transmission rates, any costs collected under such 
retail “financial commitments” would need to also be credited to the wholesale transmission 
revenue requirement for the applicable TO Zone to ensure that the costs of any transmission 
facilities built by the transmission owner to accommodate such large loads, as planned and 
contracted for, are not shifted to other LSEs in the applicable PJM TO Zone. As Buckeye has 
14 Buckeye December 2024 Comments at 4-9; Buckeye April 2025 Comments at 10-12.

- 6 -
previously explained, the different approaches taken by AES Ohio and AEP Ohio illustrates how 
“financial commitments” at the retail level with regard to new large loads are not sufficient by 
themselves to ensure that other LSEs in the TO Zone are protected against unreasonable 
transmission cost shifts.15 Thus, additional mechanisms at the FERC-jurisdictional wholesale 
level, beyond the purely retail “financial commitments” describe by Vistra (and ACEG), are 
required to ensure just and reasonable Commission-jurisdictional transmission rates. 
As noted in Buckeye’s April 2025 Comments (at 10-12), and the additional details in our 
December 2024 Comments (at 4-9), the PJM Tariff should be revised so that each LSE is 
responsible, as part of the calculation of zonal transmission rates, for its large load demand.16 Such 
LSE responsibility will ensure that any stranded transmission costs associated with such large 
loads are not shifted to other LSEs through PJM transmission rates. Indeed, this approach would 
encourage LSEs to require financial commitments of their retail large load customers in order to 
backstop their wholesale responsibility, avoiding the issue of whether PJM should require retail 
financial commitments from large loads to host LSEs (much less the issue of where such a 
requirement should be located17). Critically, only the LSE where the large load is located has the 
ability to push stranded cost responsibility and “financial commitments” to the large retail load. 
15 Buckeye December 2024 Comments at 7-9. While both AES Ohio and AEP Ohio required certain minimum 
demand payments, backed by credit support, from large load customers for a period of time sufficient to recover 
investments in transmission facilities built to accommodate such large loads as planned and contracted for, the 
critical difference is that “AES Ohio committed to apply any payments it receives from Amazon under this 
arrangement to the wholesale transmission revenue requirement to ensure that all other wholesale transmission 
customers would similarly be held harmless from any stranded costs caused by the retail load not showing up as 
expected.” Id. at 7 (footnote omitted). AEP Ohio, on the other hand, has not yet made any such commitment, 
“leaving other wholesale transmission customers in the AEP Zone (including Buckeye) bearing the stranded 
transmission costs.” Id. at 8. 
16 The extent of such responsibility, whether 100% or something less, the length of time such responsibility would 
remain in place, and other details would be subject to further Commission proceedings.
17 As noted above, Buckeye takes no position on the dispute between Vistra and ACEG on where any such 
“financial commitment” is located. What matters for PJM rates is LSE responsibility.

- 7 -
Other LSEs that would be affected by material reduction in large loads through transmission cost-
shifting at the wholesale level have no ability whatsoever to mitigate such transmission cost-
shifting through the imposition of retail “financial commitments” on large loads located in the 
retail service territory of other LSEs. 
It is therefore imperative that the Commission take steps to mitigate the potential for 
significant shifting of transmission costs at the wholesale level to LSEs that do not have the ability 
to mitigate the effects of such cost-shifting through the imposition of “financial commitments” at 
the retail level on the large retail loads causing such cost-shifting.18  If the Commission does not 
address this issue in this proceeding, the Commission should open a separate Section 206 
proceeding to ensure the PJM Tariff contains sufficient provisions to mitigate transmission cost 
shifting caused by large loads.19  Regardless of the approach the Commission decides to take, these 
issues should be promptly addressed.20 
III.
CONCLUSION
Buckeye respectfully requests that the Commission accept and give full consideration to 
this Limited Response in connection with its examination of the issues in this proceeding.
18 Given the magnitude of the large, principally data center, loads currently being planned for by PJM transmission 
owners, and the uneven distribution of such large loads among PJM TOs and among LSEs within a PJM TO Zone, 
Commission inaction is not justified on the basis that the potential transmission costs shifting effects would be de 
minimis or that such effects, even if significant, would be evenly distributed.
19 A separate Section 206 proceeding addressing standardized transmission-level load interconnection processes, as 
suggested by Vistra, is overly broad and not necessary to address these concerns unless such a proceeding focuses 
solely on interconnection processes for large loads exceeding a certain threshold.  
20 Buckeye April 2025 Comments at 10-13.

- 8 -
